telemetry-stream.title: Numbers and text in a single stream
body: Scout Sigma is awake and transmitting its first sensor readings. The flight computer measures battery charge, altitude, and core system temperature. However, raw data arrives on the console as an unreadable continuous line.

To build a clear instrument dashboard, your code needs to combine two elements: explanatory labels in quotes and physical measurement values as numbers. C++ lets you combine them within a single statement.
In this chapter, you will learn to link data into continuous output chains using the `<<` operator, control line breaks, and annotate your code with comments that the compiler completely ignores.

more.title: Why `cout` is called `cout` and where streams came from
body: In early C, terminal output was performed by the `printf` function. Programmers had to manually specify type codes in a format string, such as `%d` for integers or `%s` for strings. If a format specifier failed to match the actual variable type, the program either crashed or corrupted memory.

When creating C++, Bjarne Stroustrup and Dave Presotto at AT&T Bell Labs introduced a fundamentally safer approach: type-safe I/O streams. The stream paradigm means that the compiler automatically inspects the type of whatever you pass to the stream and invokes the appropriate conversion routine.

The name `cout` stands for «character output» or «console output». The prefix `c` signifies its place in the C++ standard stream family (alongside `cin` for character input and `cerr` for error reporting). The `<<` operator originally served only as a bitwise left-shift in C; in C++, it was overloaded to denote the physical direction of streaming data.

sources.title: Bjarne Stroustrup — The Design and Evolution of C++ (Addison-Wesley)
Bjarne Stroustrup — A History of C++: 1979—1991 (ACM HOPL-II)

numbers-and-chaining.title: Numbers and output chaining
body: In C++, numbers are written directly without quotes. Text inside quotes like `"98"` is treated as a string of characters, whereas `98` without quotes is a numeric value that the processor can compute with.
The stream insertion operator `<<` can be called multiple times in a single statement. This technique is known as chaining. Data flows into `cout` sequentially from left to right.

In the first line, the string `"BATTERY: "` enters the stream first, followed immediately by the number `98`, then the `"%"` sign, and finally the `endl` manipulator that advances the cursor to a new line.

predict-output.title: Predict the telemetry line
body: Examine the two lines of code below. Pay close attention to spaces inside the quotation marks and where `endl` is located.
Type the exact console output. This is an exercise in spotting syntax details, not an exam — trace the data flow carefully.
predict-output.explain: On the first line, there is no space between `SOL:` and `14` because none was written inside quotes. On the second line, `C` directly follows `-18` without a space and without a trailing newline.

first-chain.title: Combine separate outputs into a chain
first-chain.task: Rewrite the three separate `cout` statements into a single statement using the `<<` chaining operator to print exactly: `SIGMA SPEED: 12 M/S`.
first-chain.hint: Start with `cout << "SIGMA SPEED: "` and continue with `<< 12 << " M/S" << endl;`. Remember the semicolon `;` at the end.
first-chain.solutionNote: All three components are now chained in a single statement with three `<<` operators.

stream-flow.title: How data travels to the screen
body: The `<<` operator acts like a conveyor belt. Each element is placed onto the stream and travels toward its destination: the terminal display. The arrival sequence is strictly determined by the left-to-right order of the `<<` operators.
The compiler automatically determines the data type of each segment: text remains text, while numeric values are converted into characters for visual rendering without manual format codes.
stream-flow.alt: Diagram: a text literal, a numeric literal, and a manipulator pass sequentially through << operators into cout and appear on the terminal.

newline-and-escape.title: The `\n` escape sequence and the `endl` manipulator
body: So far we have relied on `endl` to break lines. You can also trigger a line break using the escape sequence `\n` (newline) embedded directly inside quotation marks.

The character pair `
` is written as two characters in code, but the compiler translates it into a single control character: «move the cursor to the beginning of the next line». For example, `cout << "A
B
";` prints two lines.
Other standard escape sequences include `\t` for a horizontal tab stop, `\"` to print double quotation marks inside a string, and `\\` to output a literal backslash.

more.title: Buffering: why real-time systems prefer `\n`
body: The `endl` manipulator performs two operations: it inserts a newline character and immediately flushes the output buffer (performs `flush`).

Operating systems avoid sending output to screens or disks one character at a time because hardware I/O operations are slow. Data accumulates inside an internal memory buffer before being flushed in large blocks. If a flight loop calls `endl` thousands of times, the system is forced into continuous synchronous hardware writes, dropping throughput dramatically.

In high-performance flight systems, `\n` is the default choice for newlines. The `endl` manipulator is reserved for situations where output must appear on screen immediately before a potentially critical failure.

escape-practice.title: Two lines in one statement
escape-practice.task:
Write a program that prints two lines to the terminal using ONLY ONE `cout` statement and `\n` escape characters:
`SIGMA SENSORS: OK`
`DRIFT: 0`
escape-practice.hint:
Embed `
` between the sensor status and `DRIFT`, and also at the very end: `cout << "SIGMA SENSORS: OK
DRIFT: 0
";`
escape-practice.solutionNote: A single `cout` statement with embedded `\n` produces two distinct lines in the console without `endl`.

comments-guide.title: Mission log notes: comments
body: Comments are explanatory notes for human engineers. The compiler discards them entirely — comments consume zero memory and have no effect on execution speed.
A single-line comment starts with two forward slashes `//`. Everything following them on that line is ignored by the compiler. It is typically used for inline notes.

A multi-line comment starts with `/*` and ends with `*/`. Everything between these markers is treated as a comment across any number of lines. Note: C++ does not allow nesting multi-line comments inside each other.

find-comment-bug.title: Find the defective comment
body: A syntax error in Sigma's telemetry code caused compilation to fail. Find and click on the line containing the mistake.
find-comment-bug.explain: Line 7 opens a multi-line comment `/*` that is never closed with `*/`. Consequently, the compiler absorbed the `return` statement and reported «unterminated /* comment».

fill-telemetry.title: Restore the pressure telemetry
body: Three connection elements were lost from the telemetry output line. Fill in the missing gaps so the program prints atmospheric pressure correctly.
fill-telemetry.explain: Operators `<<` join text and numbers, while `endl` or `'\n'` terminates the line.

telemetry-dashboard.title: Build Sigma's telemetry dashboard
telemetry-dashboard.task:
Write a complete program that outputs a clean 5-line telemetry dashboard. Print numeric values without quotes using `<<` chaining. Include at least two single-line comments `//`:
--- TELEMETRY: SIGMA ---
ALTITUDE: 24 M
BATTERY: 91%
CORE TEMP: -12 C
STATUS: OPERATIONAL
telemetry-dashboard.hint: Use a separate `cout` for each line, for example: `cout << "BATTERY: " << 91 << "%" << endl;`.

recap.title: Second mission recap
points: Numbers are written in C++ without quotation marks — the compiler recognizes them as numeric values and converts them for display.
The `<<` operator chains text, numbers, and formatting commands into a single stream from left to right.
The `\n` escape sequence breaks lines inside strings without triggering a forced buffer flush, unlike `endl`.
Comments (`//` and `/* ... */`) document software logic and are completely stripped during compilation.
Currently, all metrics in our dashboard are hardcoded constants. To store and update live values during flight, the next lesson introduces variables and data types.
